You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo current source: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$.
    *   Piezo capacitance $C_p \approx 25\text{ nF}$.
    *   Target: $V_{out} \in [1.8, 3.6]\text{ V}$.
    *   Ripple: $\le 50\text{ mV}$.
    *   Startup: $\le 0.4\text{ s}$.
    *   Settled: $\Delta V \le 20\text{ mV}$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, $R_L$).
    *   $V_{oc}$ is low (3.2 V nominal), meaning diode drops (0.25 V for DSCH) are significant.

    *   Proposed a "PSSHI_FBR_Zener" (Parallel SSHI with Full Bridge Rectifier and Zener).
    *   Components: L1, S1 (SYNC), D1-D4 (Full Bridge), Dz (Zener), Cout.
    *   The SSHI part (L1+S1) was in parallel with the piezo.
    *   The rectifier (D1-D4) converted the piezo voltage to DC.
    *   *Result:* Failed almost everything. $V_{out}$ settled way too low (around 0.9 V).
    *   *Why?* The SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) normally works by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks. However, the layout in the previous design put a full bridge *after* the piezo. In a standard SSHI, the inductor is used to invert the voltage on $C_p$, and then a rectifier is used to extract the energy. If the bridge is connected directly to the piezo terminals, it might be clamping the voltage or creating paths that interfere with the L-S inversion.
    *   Actually, looking at the circuit: `D1 pzp out`, `D2 pzn out`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`. This is a standard bridge. The SSHI part `L1 pzp n1`, `S1 n1 pzn` is in parallel with the piezo.
    *   The problem: In the previous design, the bridge is always active. When S1 closes, the inductor L1 is connected between pzp and pzn. But the bridge diodes also provide paths. More importantly, the bridge diodes have a forward voltage drop. For $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$, a full bridge (2 diodes in path) drops $\approx 0.5\text{ V}$.
    *   The "PSSHI" attempt failed because the power extraction wasn't efficient enough or the inversion wasn't working as intended.

    *   SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is far superior to simple rectification for low $V_{oc}$ piezo harvesters.
    *   *Topology:*
        1.  Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Storage Capacitor ($C_{out}$).
        2.  Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ are used to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   Wait, the standard SSHI typically uses a "flipping" circuit *before* the rectifier.
    *   Let's try a standard SSHI approach:
        *   The piezo is connected to a rectifier.
        *   The inductor is connected in parallel with the piezo, switched at the peaks.
        *   Wait, if the inductor is in parallel with the piezo, the switch S closes to create an LC resonant circuit that flips the voltage $V_{Cp}$.
        *   Connectivity: Piezo (pzp, pzn). Rectifier diodes connect (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0). Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ connect (pzp, pzn) in parallel.
        *   Let's refine:
            *   $L$ connects pzp to $n_1$.
            *   $S$ connects $n_1$ to pzn.
            *   Diodes: $D_1$ [pzp, out], $D_2$ [pzn, out], $D_3$ [0, pzp], $D_4$ [0, pzn]. (Full bridge).
            *   This is exactly what was proposed in PSSHI_FBR_Zener. Why did it fail?
            *   Looking at the results: $V_{avg}$ was very low.
            *   Maybe $C_{out}$ was too small? $2.2 \mu\text{F}$ is usually enough, but $22 \mu\text{F}$ (the value in the failed design was $2.2\text{e-05}$ which is $22 \mu\text{F}$, no wait $2.2\text{e-05}$ is $22 \mu\text{F}$, let me re-read: `Cout C out 0 2.2e-05` $\rightarrow 22 \mu\text{F}$).
            *   Check the energy: $I_p = 50 \mu\text{A}, f = 100\text{ Hz}, C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
            *   Power available: $P \approx \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 f \times \text{efficiency}$.
            *   $V_{oc} = \frac{50\mu}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{n}} \approx 3.18\text{ V}$.
            *   $P_{avail} \approx 0.5 \cdot 25\text{n} \cdot 3.18^2 \cdot 100 \approx 12.6 \mu\text{W}$.
            *   Load $R_L = 330\text{ k}\Omega$. At $V_{out} = 2\text{ V}$, $P_{load} = V^2/R = 4 / 330\text{k} \approx 12.1 \mu\text{W}$.
            *   It's very tight! Diode drops in a full bridge (0.5 V) will kill the efficiency.
            *   We need a more efficient rectifier. A half-bridge or a synchronous rectifier? (But we only have 2 SYNCs).

    *   Instead of a full bridge, use a half-bridge if we can bias the piezo. But the piezo is a current source.
    *   A half-bridge rectifier (1 diode) is only possible if we can ground one terminal (pzn) or provide a DC bias.
    *   Since we can't easily bias without a voltage source, we must use a full bridge or an SSHI with better extraction.
    *   Wait, the SSHI voltage flipping *increases* the voltage seen by the rectifier.
    *   The standard SSHI flipping:
        *   $V_{Cp}$ reaches $V_{max}$.
        *   Switch closes, $V_{Cp}$ flips to $-V_{max}$.
        *   Then $V_{Cp}$ rises back to $V_{max}$.
        *   Total $\Delta V$ per half cycle is $2 V_{max}$.
    *   The rectifier diodes must be low-drop. DSCH is used.
    *   If $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$ and $V_{out} = 1.8\text{ V}$, the bridge diodes ($2 \times 0.25\text{ V} = 0.5\text{ V}$) are a significant loss.

    *   Let's try a different topology: **SEH (Synchronous Electric Harvesting)** or a variation.
    *   Actually, a simpler way to improve on FBR is to use a **Charge Pump** or a **Voltage Multiplier**, but the $V_{oc}$ is already high enough if we can just avoid the double diode drop.
    *   Wait, if we use a **Half-Bridge** and a capacitor to bias the piezo:
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Capacitor $C_{bias}$ from pzn to 0.
        *   Diode $D_1$ from pzp to out.
        *   This way, only one diode drop. But $C_{bias}$ must be large.
        *   However, the piezo is a current source. The voltage at pzn will float to $V_{out} - V_d$ during the positive half and then... no, that's not right.

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Rectifier** using the SYNC controllers.
        *   We have 2 SYNCs.
        *   SYNC 1: Switch $S_1$ from pzp to out.
        *   SYNC 2: Switch $S_2$ from pzn to out.
        *   This would be a synchronous half-wave rectifier.
        *   But we need to handle the negative half-cycle too.
        *   Actually, we can use the SYNCs to implement a **Synchronous Rectifier**:
            *   $S_1$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ out) closed when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.
            *   $S_2$ (pzn $\rightarrow$ out) closed when $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$.
            *   This eliminates diode drops!
            *   $S_1$: `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`.
            *   $S_2$: `edges="neg"`, `phase=0`.
            *   This acts as a full-wave rectifier without the diodes.

    *   Now, can we add the SSHI inductor to this?
        *   We only have 2 SYNCs. If we use them for rectification, we can't use them for the L-C flip.
        *   But maybe synchronous rectification is enough?
        *   Let's check power: $P_{avail} \approx 12.6 \mu\text{W}$. $P_{load} \approx 12.1 \mu\text{W}$.
        *   With synchronous rectification, efficiency $\approx 90\%+$. This should work.
        *   With FBR (diode drops), efficiency $\approx \frac{V_{oc} - 0.5}{V_{oc}} \approx \frac{2.7}{3.2} \approx 84\%$.
        *   Wait, $12.6 \cdot 0.84 = 10.5 \mu\text{W}$, which is less than $12.1 \mu\text{W}$. This explains why FBR failed.

    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Rectifier** (SR) as a first proposal.
    *   $S_1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ out, `ctrl=G1`, `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`.
    *   $S_2$: pzn $\rightarrow$ out, `ctrl=G2`, `edges="neg"`, `phase=0`.
    *   Wait, there's a catch: for the current to flow from pzp to out, pzp must be higher than out. The SYNC closes at the peak.
    *   But we also need a path for the return current.
    *   The piezo is a current source. In the positive half, $I$ flows pzp $\rightarrow$ pzn.
    *   If we connect $S_1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ out, then the current flows pzp $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn.
    *   This means pzn must be connected to 0.
    *   But pzn is the other terminal of the piezo. If we connect it to 0, we can't use $S_2$ to connect pzn $\rightarrow$ out.
    *   Correct Synchronous Rectifier for a current source:
        *   Positive half: $S_1$ connects pzp to out, $S_3$ connects pzn to 0.
        *   Negative half: $S_2$ connects pzn to out, $S_4$ connects pzp to 0.
        *   This requires 4 switches. We only have 4. But we only have 2 SYNCs.
        *   A SYNC can control multiple switches if they are the same? No, the `ctrl` field is a string, and the SYNC definition doesn't specify it can be shared. Actually, let's check: "closes its switches". This implies one SYNC can control multiple switches.
        *   If G1 controls $S_1$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ out) and $S_3$ (pzn $\rightarrow$ 0), and G2 controls $S_2$ (pzn $\rightarrow$ out) and $S_4$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ 0).
        *   G1: `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`.
        *   G2: `edges="neg"`, `phase=0`.

    *   Actually, a simpler way to get a return path is to use diodes.
        *   $S_1$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ out), $S_2$ (pzn $\rightarrow$ out).
        *   $D_3$ (0 $\rightarrow$ pzp), $D_4$ (0 $\rightarrow$ pzn).
        *   This is a "hybrid" rectifier.
        *   Positive half: $S_1$ is closed, current flows pzp $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow D_4 \rightarrow$ pzn.
        *   Negative half: $S_2$ is closed, current flows pzn $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow D_3 \rightarrow$ pzp.
        *   Only one diode drop per half cycle (DSCH: 0.25 V).
        *   Efficiency: $\frac{V_{oc} - 0.25}{V_{oc}} \approx \frac{2.93}{3.2} \approx 91\%$.
        *   $12.6 \cdot 0.91 = 11.4 \mu\text{W}$. Still very close to $12.1 \mu\text{W}$.

    *   Let's rethink. We need more power. The only way to get more power from a piezo is to use **SSHI** (the voltage flip).
    *   SSHI with a Bridge:
        *   $L$ and $S_{flip}$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) to extract the power.
        *   This is what PSSHI_FBR_Zener was. Why did it fail?
        *   Maybe the `ton` and `phase` were wrong? Or the L value?
        *   $L$ should be chosen so that the flip happens quickly. $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   For $L=10\text{ mH}, C_p=25\text{ nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 15.7 \mu\text{s}$.
        *   The failed design had `ton = 49.7 uS`. That's too long; it would flip the voltage and then flip it back.
        *   Also, the `phase` was 0. The peak of the voltage occurs at the zero crossing of the current. The SYNC triggers at the zero crossing. So `phase=0` is correct for the voltage peak.

    *   Wait! The PSSHI_FBR_Zener failed with $V_{out} \approx 0.9\text{ V}$. This suggests that the energy was not being transferred to the capacitor.
    *   Looking at the components: `D1 pzp out`, `D2 pzn out`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`. This is a bridge.
    *   When $S_1$ (the flip switch) closes, $L_1$ is in parallel with the piezo.
    *   Wait, if the bridge is there, then $L_1$ is also in parallel with the bridge!
    *   During the flip, the current flows through $L_1$ and $C_p$. But it can also flow through the diodes.
    *   Actually, if $V_{out}$ is $0.9\text{ V}$, and the bridge is connected, the diodes $D_1/D_3$ or $D_2/D_4$ might be conducting during the flip, dampening the resonance.
    *   The correct way to do SSHI is to have the flip switch *independent* of the rectifier or to use a more complex arrangement.
